newsitem.title: NEPAL: Nepal reduces fuel price hike ahead of parliament.
newsitem.headline: Nepal reduces fuel price hike ahead of parliament.

text.p: Strong protests from coalition partners forced the Nepali government on Tuesday to cut back a recent increase in fuel prices two days ahead of a parliamentary debate, state radio said.
"His majesty's government has instructed Nepal Oil Corporation to make some reductions in the recently increased prices of products like kerosene, diesel, and cooking gas," state Radio said.
It said the government rolled back prices of diesel by 11.4 percent and kerosene by 4.5 percent.
On June 13 the Nepali government raised the domestic price of diesel by 25 percent, kerosene by 15.7 percent and petrol by 14.7 percent.
The government has decided not to cut back the price of petrol, the state radio said.
The fuel price hike had sparked widespread protests and criticism of the three-month-old coalition government, comprising of communists and former royalists.
The decision to roll back the prices was expected to calm the coalition partners who intended to grill the government in the parliament over the price hike.

Earlier on Tuesday Pradeep Nepal, a central committee member of the communist Unified Marxist-Leninist (UML) party, which dominates the ruling coalition told Reuters the UML was unhappy with the fuel price hike decision.

"The government will face more criticism from the ruling benches than from the opposition," Nepal said. "The biggest battle (with the government) over the oil price hike will be in the parliament," he added.
The parliament is set to convene on Thursday to debate the budget for the 1997/98 fiscal year, beginning on July 16.
Nepali truck and bus owners had threatened to raise fares by up to 35 percent unless the price hike was reversed.
About 800 housewives protested against the price increase last week, demanding the government reconsider its decision.

The government said it raised the prices to aid the loss-making state-owned Nepal Oil Corp. The firm, which has a monopoly over the import and distribution of petroleum products in Nepal, had been losing about 30 million rupees ($525,400) a month since last October because of subsidies.
But the communists fear the move, which came in the wake of their victory in local council elections, could jeopardise the party's political prospects.

The UML is the largest party in parliament, controlling 90 seats in the 205-member lower house. Chand's Rastriya Prajatantra Party has 20 deputies and the opposition Nepali Congress has 87 seats. ($1 = 57.1 rupees)
